Forms the forehead and part of the roof of the eye sockets. It contributes to the protective wall around the brain.
Paired bone forming much of the roof and sides of the cranial vault. The two parietal bones meet at the sagittal suture.
Forms part of the side and base of the skull. It houses the structures of hearing and balance and articulates with the mandible.
Forms the back and part of the base of the skull. Its large opening, the foramen magnum, connects the cranial cavity to the vertebral canal.
Central bone of the skull base, contributing to the orbits. Its sella turcica contains the pituitary fossa.
Located between the orbits, it contributes to the nasal cavity and nasal septum. Its cribriform plate is crossed by olfactory nerve fibres.
Paired bone of the upper jaw. It carries the upper teeth and contributes to the hard palate and the floor of the orbit.
Bone of the lower jaw, carrying the lower teeth. Its joints with the temporal bones allow opening and movement of the jaw.
Forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the orbit. It also contributes to the zygomatic arch.
One of the two small bones forming the bony bridge of the nose. Much of the projecting nose is supported by cartilage.
Small bone on the medial wall of the orbit, associated with the passage that drains tears towards the nasal cavity.
Contributes to the rear of the hard palate and to the walls of the nasal cavity and orbit.
Curved bone projecting into the nasal cavity. Its mucosal covering helps condition inhaled air. It is a separate bone from the ethmoid.
Thin midline bone forming part of the nasal septum, which separates the right and left nasal cavities.
Located in the neck below the mandible. Suspended by muscles and ligaments, it supports attachments involved in tongue movement and swallowing.
Middle-ear ossicle attached to the eardrum. It transmits vibration to the incus. Its individual 3D mesh is absent from this dataset.
Middle-ear ossicle between the malleus and stapes, forming part of the sound-transmission chain. Its individual 3D mesh is absent from this dataset.
Middle-ear ossicle whose footplate transmits vibration at the oval window of the inner ear. Its individual 3D mesh is absent from this dataset.
First cervical vertebra, supporting the skull. Its ring-like shape differs from a typical vertebra; it articulates with the occipital bone and the axis.
Second cervical vertebra. Its upward projection, the dens, forms a pivot involved in rotation of the atlas and head.
One of the seven vertebrae of the neck. The cervical spine supports the head, allows movement and surrounds the upper vertebral canal.
One of the twelve thoracic vertebrae. These vertebrae articulate with the ribs and form the spinal part of the thoracic cage.
One of the five lumbar vertebrae in the lower back. Their large bodies bear substantial load above the sacrum.
Bone formed by fusion of five sacral vertebrae. It links the vertebral column to the hip bones through the sacroiliac joints.
Terminal part of the vertebral column, below the sacrum, formed from a variable number of small vertebrae. No separately identified mesh is supplied in this dataset.
Midline bone at the front of the chest. It comprises the manubrium, body and xiphoid process. Here the three source meshes are selected together as one adult bone.
A rib from pairs 1–7. Its costal cartilage attaches directly to the sternum. Costal cartilage is not shown in this bone layer.
A rib from pairs 8–10. Its cartilage joins the cartilage above rather than attaching directly to the sternum. The cartilage is not shown here.
A rib from pairs 11–12. Its anterior end has no attachment to the sternum; posteriorly it articulates with the thoracic spine.
Links the sternum to the scapula. It helps hold the shoulder away from the thorax and transmits forces from the upper limb.
Flat bone at the back of the thorax. Its glenoid cavity receives the head of the humerus; its surfaces provide many muscle attachments.
Long bone of the arm between shoulder and elbow. It articulates with the scapula above and with the radius and ulna below.
Forearm bone on the thumb side in anatomical position. It participates in the wrist joint and rotates around the ulna during pronation and supination.
Forearm bone on the little-finger side in anatomical position. Its olecranon forms the bony point of the elbow.
One of the eight carpal bones of each wrist. Together they form two rows between the forearm and the metacarpals.
Carpal bone on the thumb side of the proximal row. It articulates with the radius and connects the two carpal rows through its articulations.
Central bone of the proximal carpal row, between the scaphoid and triquetral. It articulates with the radius above and the capitate below.
Carpal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row. The pisiform lies on its palmar surface.
Small sesamoid carpal bone within the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris. It lies in front of the triquetral and is included in the conventional 206 bones.
Carpal bone at the base of the thumb. Its saddle-shaped joint with the first metacarpal contributes to the mobility of the thumb.
Small bone of the distal carpal row, between the trapezium and capitate. It lies mainly beneath the base of the second metacarpal.
Largest carpal bone, situated near the centre of the wrist. It belongs to the distal row and aligns mainly with the third metacarpal.
Bone on the little-finger side of the distal carpal row. Its palmar hook provides an attachment for the flexor retinaculum.
One of the five bones of the palm. Numbering runs from I at the thumb to V at the little finger. It lies between the carpus and a proximal phalanx.
A finger bone. Each hand has fourteen phalanges: two in the thumb and three in each other finger. Proximal, middle and distal indicate increasing distance from the palm.
Pelvic bone formed by fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis. Its acetabulum receives the femoral head; posteriorly it meets the sacrum.
Long bone of the thigh between hip and knee. Its head articulates with the acetabulum; its lower end articulates with the tibia and patella.
Sesamoid bone within the quadriceps tendon at the front of the knee. It contributes to the mechanical action of the knee extensor apparatus.
Medial bone of the leg and its main weight-bearing bone. It articulates with the femur at the knee and the talus at the ankle.
Slender bone on the lateral side of the leg. Its lower end forms the lateral malleolus and contributes to ankle stability.
Tarsal bone between the leg and the rest of the foot. It receives load from the tibia and articulates with the calcaneus and navicular.
Heel bone, beneath the talus. Its posterior surface receives the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
One of the seven tarsal bones of each foot. The tarsus links the ankle region to the metatarsals and contributes to the arches of the foot.
Medial tarsal bone between the talus and the three cuneiform bones. It contributes to the medial longitudinal arch of the foot.
Lateral tarsal bone between the calcaneus and the fourth and fifth metatarsals. It contributes to the lateral column of the foot.
Largest of the three cuneiforms. It lies between the navicular and the first metatarsal, on the big-toe side of the foot.
Middle and smallest cuneiform, between the medial and lateral cuneiforms. It lies behind the base of the second metatarsal.
Lateral member of the three cuneiform bones. It lies between the navicular and the third metatarsal, next to the cuboid.
One of the five metatarsal bones. Numbering runs from I at the big toe to V at the little toe. It lies between the tarsus and a proximal phalanx.
A toe bone. Each foot has fourteen phalanges: two in the big toe and three in each other toe. They form the articulated skeleton of the toes.
Two sesamoid bones beneath the head of the first metatarsal, shown as one selectable group. These additional sesamoids are outside the conventional 206-bone count.
Permanent front tooth with an edge adapted to cutting food. Teeth contain enamel and dentine; they are not bones and are counted separately in this atlas.
Permanent tooth between the incisors and premolars, with a pointed crown. Teeth are shown separately from the skeletal bone count.
Permanent tooth between the canine and molars, contributing to crushing food. There are two premolars per quadrant in the usual adult dentition.
Posterior tooth with a broad chewing surface. This dataset includes the first and second permanent molars; wisdom teeth are not supplied.
An extraocular muscle: coordinated contractions steer the eyeball within the orbit.
Raises the upper eyelid to open the eye.
An extrinsic tongue muscle, contributing to positioning the tongue for speech and swallowing.
Part of the soft palate musculature, which changes its position and shape during swallowing and speech.
A neck muscle involved in positioning or stabilizing the head and cervical spine.
Located above the hyoid; this group participates in hyoid movement, swallowing and opening the jaw.
An infrahyoid muscle, helping position the hyoid or larynx during swallowing and vocal activity.
An intrinsic laryngeal muscle. This group controls the vocal folds and the opening of the larynx.
A pharyngeal muscle involved in the coordinated passage of a swallowed bolus.
A thin superficial neck muscle that tenses the skin and contributes to lower-face movements.
A lateral neck muscle connecting cervical vertebrae to upper ribs; contributes to neck movement and accessory inspiration.
Part of the deep back musculature, which supports posture and controls movements between vertebrae.
A muscular partition between thorax and abdomen. Its contraction lowers its dome and increases thoracic volume during inspiration.
Muscles occupying the spaces between ribs. Their layers stabilize the intercostal spaces and participate in breathing.
Muscle attached to the rib cage. Its shape and relations can be examined by hiding the overlying structures.
A broad abdominal wall muscle, contributing to trunk movement and compression of the abdominal contents.
A shoulder-girdle muscle, helping position or stabilize the scapula or clavicle during upper-limb movement.
A muscle acting at the shoulder, helping move the humerus relative to the shoulder girdle.
One of the rotator cuff muscles; helps keep the humeral head centred against the glenoid during shoulder movement.
An anterior arm muscle contributing to elbow flexion and forearm supination. Its two heads join distally.
An elbow flexor, bringing the forearm toward the arm.
Contributes to extending the elbow and stabilizing the joint.
Turns the forearm into pronation, with the radius crossing in front of the ulna.
Turns the forearm into supination, bringing the radius and ulna toward a parallel position.
A forearm muscle contributing to wrist flexion or tension of the palmar tissues.
An extensor of the wrist, also contributing to lateral balance of the hand.
A long finger flexor. Its tendons transmit force from the forearm to the fingers.
A finger extensor whose tendons continue from the forearm toward the hand.
A muscle controlling the thumb. Thumb movements combine flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and opposition across several joints.
An intrinsic hand muscle, contributing to the fine positioning of the fingers during grip.
A pelvic floor muscle, contributing to support of the pelvic contents and continence.
A striated muscle surrounding the anal canal, contributing to voluntary anal continence.
A deep hip muscle, contributing to external rotation and stabilization of the femoral head.
Part of the iliopsoas group, which flexes the hip and contributes to lumbopelvic stability.
A gluteal muscle. This group moves the hip and stabilizes the pelvis, notably during walking and single-leg stance.
A muscle of the medial thigh, contributing to drawing the thigh toward the body midline.
A posterior thigh muscle contributing to knee flexion. Most parts of this group also cross the hip.
Part of the quadriceps femoris, the main extensor of the knee. Rectus femoris also crosses the hip.
A long superficial thigh muscle crossing the hip and knee, contributing to hip flexion and knee flexion.
Tenses the fascia lata through the iliotibial tract and contributes to stabilization of the hip and knee.
A posterior leg muscle contributing to plantar flexion, which raises the heel or points the foot downward.
A small posterior knee muscle that helps unlock the knee at the start of flexion.
A lateral or anterior leg muscle contributing to eversion of the foot.
Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot; helps control lowering of the foot after heel contact.
Contributes to inversion and plantar flexion of the foot and supports the medial longitudinal arch.
An extensor of the toes or hallux, helping raise the digits of the foot.
A flexor of the toes or hallux, contributing to support and propulsion through the foot.
An intrinsic foot muscle, contributing to toe positioning and support of the foot during loading.
Superficial scalp muscle, involved in movements of the scalp and facial expression.
Facial muscle acting around the nose, involved in movements of the nostrils or upper lip.
Part of the circular muscle around the eye, which closes the eyelids.
Muscle surrounding the mouth opening. It closes and shapes the lips during speech and facial expression.
Pulls the corner of the mouth upward and outward, contributing to a smile.
Raises the upper lip, contributing to facial expression.
Facial muscle in the brow region, contributing to frowning and movement of the skin between the eyebrows.
Lowers part of the lower lip or the corner of the mouth during facial expression.
Raises the upper lip or corner of the mouth during facial expression.
Draws the corner of the mouth sideways.
Raises the skin of the chin and helps protrude the lower lip.
Compresses the cheek against the teeth and helps keep food between the chewing surfaces.
A chewing muscle that elevates the mandible to close the jaw. Its superficial and deep portions are separately selectable.
Deep chewing muscle participating in coordinated movements of the mandible.
Fan-shaped chewing muscle at the temple, helping elevate and retract the mandible.

Fibrocartilaginous structure between adjacent vertebral bodies. It distributes loads and allows small movements. The atlas shows the outer surface only; the annulus fibrosus and nucleus pulposus are not separately modelled.

Cartilaginous extension of a rib, contributing to the flexibility of the front of the rib cage during breathing. This layer contains the source structures labelled for ribs 1 to 7 on each side; cartilages of ribs 8 to 10 are not separately available.
Supports the flexible part of the external nose or the front of the nasal septum. Its shape helps define the nasal passages.
Ring-shaped cartilage below the thyroid cartilage, supporting the larynx above the trachea. It has an anterior arch and a broader posterior lamina.
Large protective cartilage at the front and sides of the larynx. It provides attachment for laryngeal structures and contributes to the framework around the vocal folds.
Paired laryngeal cartilage on the upper part of the cricoid. Its movements help adjust the position of the vocal folds.
Small paired cartilage supporting soft tissues around the entrance to the larynx.

C-shaped fibrocartilage on the inner part of the tibial plateau, between the tibia and femur. It helps distribute loads and improves joint congruence. Its peripheral attachments to the capsule and medial collateral ligament make it less mobile than the lateral meniscus. These attachments are not modelled here.

Curved fibrocartilage on the outer part of the tibial plateau, between the tibia and femur. It helps distribute loads and accommodate the femoral condyle during knee movement. It is generally more mobile than the medial meniscus. The atlas shows its outer shape; fibres and vascular zones are not represented.
Muscular pump connecting pulmonary and systemic circulation. This selection groups the atrial and ventricular walls; valves, coronary vessels and chamber contents are not included.
Large abdominal gland involved in metabolism, storage and bile production. The source parenchymal parts are grouped into one selectable organ; internal vessels and bile ducts are omitted.
Muscular tube carrying swallowed food from the pharynx to the stomach. It crosses the thorax and passes through the diaphragm.
Expandable digestive organ below the diaphragm. It stores and mixes food with gastric secretions before gradually passing it to the duodenum. Only its external surface is shown.
First part of the small intestine, receiving gastric contents, bile and pancreatic secretions.
Small-intestinal loops important for nutrient absorption, between the duodenum and ileum.
Final part of the small intestine, continuing absorption before the ileocecal junction.
Pouch at the beginning of the large intestine. The source groups it with the ileocecal junction.
Narrow blind-ended structure attached to the cecum, containing lymphoid tissue.
Part of the large intestine involved in water absorption and stool formation.
Pelvic part of the digestive tract that temporarily stores stool before defecation.
Gland behind the stomach. It supplies digestive secretions to the small intestine and releases hormones including insulin and glucagon into the blood.
Stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver, then releases it into the digestive tract. It does not produce bile.
Lymphoid organ in the upper left abdomen. It filters blood, contributes to immune responses and removes ageing blood cells.
Retroperitoneal organ that forms urine and helps regulate water, electrolytes and acid–base balance. This mesh shows the outer shape; nephrons and collecting structures are not represented.
Muscular conduit carrying urine from the kidney to the bladder. It extends through the abdomen into the pelvis.
Expandable muscular reservoir storing urine before emptying through the urethra. Its shape varies with filling.
Passage carrying urine from the bladder to the exterior. In this male model it also serves as the final route for semen.
Endocrine gland above a kidney. Its cortex and medulla produce different hormones involved in stress responses and physiological regulation; these internal regions are not separately modelled.
Lymphoid organ behind the sternum, where T lymphocytes mature. It is larger in childhood and undergoes substantial fatty replacement with age.
Airway connecting the larynx to the main bronchi. Its cartilaginous support helps maintain an open passage for air.
Main airway entering a lung and dividing into smaller bronchi. This selection shows the principal source conduit, not the complete branching tree.
Muscular organ contributing to food handling, swallowing, speech and taste. Its external surface is shown; the surrounding tongue muscles belong to the muscular layer.
Gland producing saliva, which moistens the mouth and food and contributes to digestion and oral protection.
Endocrine gland at the base of the brain, linked to the hypothalamus. Its hormones participate in growth, reproduction and regulation of other endocrine glands.
Gland below the bladder surrounding the beginning of the male urethra. Its secretions contribute to seminal fluid.
Gonad in the scrotum producing sperm and hormones, including testosterone. Internal seminiferous tubules are not modelled.
Coiled duct associated with the testis, involved in sperm maturation and storage.
Paired gland behind the bladder whose secretion contributes to seminal fluid.

Erectile tissue contributing to penile rigidity as it fills with blood. The two corpora cavernosa are grouped in this source surface. This is not a separately dissected skeletal muscle; microscopic smooth muscle is not resolved.

Erectile tissue surrounding the spongy urethra and continuing distally into the glans, which is separately selectable here. The bulbospongiosus muscle covering its root is absent from the imported muscle sources.
Distal expansion of the corpus spongiosum. The external urethral opening is at its tip. This surface does not include the foreskin, fine nerves or microscopic tissue structure.

One lobe of a lung. The right lung has three lobes and the left has two. Gas exchange occurs in microscopic alveoli, which are not individually represented. Each lobe can be hidden to inspect deeper structures.
Endocrine gland at the front of the lower neck, with two lobes joined by an isthmus. Its hormones help regulate metabolism and development. It is distinct from the thyroid cartilage of the larynx.
Paired muscle of the anterior abdominal wall extending from the pubis towards the lower thorax. It contributes to trunk flexion and abdominal compression.
Deep, mostly transverse muscle layer of the anterolateral abdominal wall. It compresses the abdominal contents and contributes to control of the trunk.

Posterior abdominal wall muscle connecting the iliac crest, lumbar transverse processes and twelfth rib. Its fibres have variable arrangements; its contribution to lumbar movement is modest relative to the main spinal muscles.

Small triangular muscle in front of the lower rectus abdominis. Its presence varies between people; it is generally associated with tension of the linea alba, although its precise function remains uncertain.
Tough outer coat forming the white of the eye. It encloses most of the globe and provides attachments for the eye muscles.
Transparent anterior surface of the eye. Its curvature contributes to focusing incoming light onto the retina.
Pigmented diaphragm surrounding the pupil. Its muscles vary the size of this opening and regulate the amount of light entering the eye.
Transparent lens behind the iris. Changes in its curvature contribute to accommodation, allowing the eye to focus at different distances.
Vascular, pigmented coat between the sclera and retina. It supplies the outer retina and absorbs stray light.

Light-sensitive neural lining at the back of the eye. Photoreceptors initiate signals that pass through retinal circuits and then the optic nerve. Its microscopic cell layers are not individually modelled.

Folded anterior region of the ciliary body containing the ciliary processes, associated with aqueous-humour production and the attachment of zonular fibres. The source does not model the whole ciliary body separately.
Fine suspensory fibres connecting the ciliary region to the lens capsule. They transmit tension involved in accommodation.
Transparent gel occupying the cavity behind the lens and in front of the retina. This mesh marks its volume, not a solid tissue wall.
Space between the cornea and iris containing aqueous humour. The source represents the cavity volume, not an additional membrane.
Gland in the upper outer orbit producing the aqueous component of tears. Tears wet and protect the eye surface.
Collecting part of the tear-drainage pathway near the inner corner of the eye. It receives the canaliculi and continues into the nasolacrimal duct.
Drainage conduit carrying tears from the lacrimal sac towards the nasal cavity.
Small drainage channels connecting the lacrimal puncta of the eyelids to the lacrimal sac. The source groups the upper and lower branches on each side.
Small collection of tears at the inner corner of the eye, near the openings of the drainage pathway. This is a fluid space, not a gland.
Dense connective-tissue support within an eyelid. It gives the lid its shape; it is neither bone nor cartilage.
Fibrous attachment linking a rectus muscle sheath to the orbital wall and contributing to support of the eye.
Fibrous pulley in the upper inner orbit that redirects the tendon of the superior oblique muscle.
Tendinous expansion transmitting the pull of the levator muscle to the upper eyelid. Only the right-side source mesh is available in this selection.
The auricles collect sound towards the external auditory canals. Both sides share one source mesh here. The eardrums, middle-ear ossicles and inner-ear structures are not included in this surface.
Cortical association region integrating information across distributed networks. Its visible surface does not delimit a single isolated function.
Frontal cortical region contributing to planning and behavioural control; functions depend on its connections with other regions.
Temporal cortical region involved in sensory processing and association. Auditory, visual and memory networks occupy distinct but connected regions.
Medial cortical region connected with networks for memory, emotion and behaviour.
Cortex concealed within the lateral sulcus, associated with taste and processing of bodily signals.
Posterior cerebral lobe containing visual cortex. Visual perception also recruits networks beyond this lobe.
The postcentral gyrus contains primary somatosensory cortex, receiving information such as touch and body position.
The precentral gyrus contains primary motor cortex, contributing to commands for voluntary movement.
Bundle carrying signals between cerebral cortex and deeper nervous structures. Individual axons are not resolved.
White-matter connection crossing the midline to link structures on the two sides.
White-matter pathway connecting structures involved in memory and emotional processing.
Deep cerebral nucleus participating in circuits that regulate movement selection and other aspects of behaviour.
Medial temporal structure important for forming memories and spatial representation.
Group of deep temporal nuclei participating in emotional processing and learning.
Diencephalic relay linking cortical, sensory and motor networks. Its many nuclei are grouped in this surface.
Diencephalic region coordinating autonomic and endocrine regulation and contributing to homeostasis.
Diencephalic structure connected with circuits for memory or emotional and motivational processing.
Small endocrine structure of the epithalamus secreting melatonin and contributing to circadian timing.
Midline forebrain structure bordering the ventricular region. The surface model does not resolve its microscopic organization.
Structure of the visual pathway beyond the retina. At the optic chiasm, nasal retinal fibres cross the midline.
Relay or connecting bundle of the central auditory pathway.
Upper brainstem region traversed by sensory and motor pathways and involved in orienting responses.
Brainstem region connecting with the cerebellum and containing pathways and nuclei involved in cranial and vital functions.
Brainstem region continuous with the spinal cord, containing ascending and descending pathways and centres involved in vital regulation.
Midbrain structure participating in the orientation of gaze and attention toward sensory events.
Coordinates movements and motor learning by comparing motor commands with sensory feedback. Both sides are grouped in this source selection.
Fold of dura mater supporting and separating nervous structures. It is a protective membrane, not neural tissue.
Representation of a cavity or passage containing cerebrospinal fluid. The coloured surface outlines a space; it is not a solid organ.
Narrow fluid-filled canal within the spinal cord. This source surface represents the canal only, not the surrounding spinal tissue.
Specialized tissue within the ventricles that contributes to cerebrospinal fluid production. The source groups the two cerebral plexuses.
Cranial nerve II carries retinal output toward the optic chiasm. Orbital and intracranial source portions are grouped per side.
Cranial nerve IV supplies the superior oblique eye muscle.
Branch of cranial nerve III, which supplies most extraocular muscles and carries parasympathetic fibres toward the ciliary ganglion.
Sensory branch belonging to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Its territory depends on the selected branch.
Fine nerve connection of the ciliary network. Short ciliary nerves convey autonomic and sensory fibres between the ganglion and the eye.
Parasympathetic relay in the orbit for pupillary constriction and accommodation. Sensory and sympathetic fibres also pass through the region.
Cranial nerve I conveys olfactory information from the nasal region. The source includes the proximal olfactory structures as a surface model.
Component of cranial nerve V, the principal sensory nerve of the face. Its mandibular division also carries motor fibres to muscles of mastication.
Component of cranial nerve VII, involved in facial movement, taste and parasympathetic functions according to the branch.
Cranial nerve VIII conveys auditory and balance information from the inner ear. Fine sensory endings are not included.
Cranial nerve IX has sensory, motor and parasympathetic components serving the pharynx, posterior tongue and related structures.
Cranial nerve X connects the brainstem with structures of the neck, thorax and abdomen. The two source meshes have unequal distal coverage.
Cranial nerve XI contributes to motor supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
Cranial nerve XII supplies most tongue muscles and contributes to tongue movement.
Cranial nerve VI supplies the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.
Part of the nerve network supplying the upper limb, formed mainly from the anterior rami C5 to T1.
Named peripheral nerve or branch of the upper limb. Motor, sensory and autonomic fibres vary by branch; microscopic terminals are not resolved.
Named peripheral nerve or branch of the lower limb, carrying signals between lumbosacral networks and its peripheral territory.
Cutaneous nerve or branch carrying sensory information from part of the skin. The surface model shows its course, not exact sensory territory boundaries.
Thoracic nerve branches following the intercostal spaces and supplying structures of the trunk wall. Multiple levels are grouped per side.
Lumbar plexus branch supplying parts of the lower abdominal wall and neighbouring regions.
Lumbar plexus nerve dividing into genital and femoral branches, serving portions of the groin and upper thigh.
Sacral plexus nerve providing somatic sensory and motor supply to the perineum. It is distinct from the pelvic autonomic nerves.
Component of the sympathetic pathway alongside the spine. The imported surfaces represent selected trunks, ganglia and connections, not the entire autonomic network.
Roots connect the spinal cord with spinal nerves; posterior roots carry sensory input and anterior roots motor output. Sensory cell bodies lie in spinal ganglia. Several levels are grouped.
Outer spinal white matter carries ascending and descending pathways. This surface surrounds separately selectable grey horns; individual tracts are not modelled as physiological connections.
Longitudinal representation of a pair of spinal grey horns. Posterior horns process sensory input; anterior horns include motor neurons. Segment-specific cellular detail is not shown.
Bundle of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots descending below the end of the spinal cord.
Midline fold of dura mater between the cerebral hemispheres. It supports and separates them without being part of the brain tissue.

Arterial vessel or named branch group carrying blood away from the heart toward its supply territory. The source surface shows the vessel course, without microscopic wall layers, capillary beds or simulated blood flow.

Venous vessel or named tributary group contributing to blood return toward the heart. Venous valves are not separately modelled. The source surface shows the vessel course, without microscopic wall layers, capillary beds or simulated blood flow.
Carries oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs. Blue is an illustrative convention. The source branching does not resolve pulmonary capillaries.
Returns oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Red is an illustrative convention. Selected tributaries are grouped with their principal source vein.
Part of the arterial supply to the heart muscle. The principal right and left coronary trees group their available source branches; additional branches remain separately selectable.
Vessel draining blood from the heart muscle. Most cardiac venous return reaches the right atrium through the coronary sinus; anterior cardiac veins can drain directly to the atrium.
Main artery leaving the left ventricle. Its ascending portion, arch and descending portion are combined here. An overlapping alternate descending surface is excluded.

Part of the venous pathway bringing blood from digestive organs toward the liver before it returns to the heart. The source surface shows the vessel course, without microscopic wall layers, capillary beds or simulated blood flow.

Venous surface in the epigastric region. Two nearly identical source variants call this trajectory superficial or superior epigastric vein. Only one surface is retained, with a local identifier; its precise branch identity remains unresolved.

Lymphoid tissue that filters lymph and supports immune responses. A named source object may contain several lymph nodes. This layer preserves those groups; collecting vessels and ducts are absent from this source file.

Lymphoid tissue at the side of the oropharynx, contributing to immune surveillance near the entrance to the digestive and respiratory tracts. Other tonsillar regions are not separately modelled in this subset.
Strong ligament on the sole connecting the calcaneus to the cuboid and metatarsal bases. It supports the longitudinal arch and forms part of the fibularis longus tendon tunnel.
Fibrous connection from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the lesser horn of the hyoid. It belongs to the suspension apparatus of the hyoid.
Fibrous attachment connecting elements of the larynx or linking them to the hyoid. These connections help support the laryngeal framework while allowing movement during swallowing and phonation.
Elastic band within the vocal fold, extending from the thyroid cartilage to the vocal process of the arytenoid. Changes in its tension contribute to pitch control.
Common distal tendon of gastrocnemius and soleus, inserting on the calcaneus. It transmits the force used in ankle plantar flexion, including walking and rising onto the toes.
Thickened lateral part of the fascia lata receiving fibres from tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus. Its distal attachment on the tibia contributes to lateral hip and knee stability.
Fibrous band spanning the carpal arch on the palmar side of the wrist. It forms the roof of the carpal tunnel containing the median nerve and finger flexor tendons.
Fibrous line of attachment shared by adjacent muscles. Pharyngeal and pterygomandibular raphes provide attachment for muscles involved in swallowing and movements of the oral cavity.

Double layer of peritoneum suspending part of the digestive tract and carrying its vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The source shows a surface envelope, without microscopic layers or all of its contents.

External body envelope. Skin provides a protective barrier, contributes to temperature regulation and contains sensory receptors. This mesh shows the external surface of the source adult male, without separate epidermis, dermis, glands or microscopic structures.
Hair is formed by keratinised cells produced in follicles within the skin. The mesh is a grouped surface representation of the source hair distribution, not a model of individual hairs or follicles.
